brief.head: Back to school at 30
brief.text: Sayyid Ahmad Khan, founder of Aligarh Muslim University, de­cided at thirty that he did not know enough, Amit Varma said, and hired six tu­tors for six sub­jects. {043-S06}

brief.head: Same tongue, same maps
brief.text: For all the talk of a world chang­ing like never be­fore, Amit Varma said, he still speaks the lan­guage he spoke as a child, under the same gov­ern­ment and maps. {#samemaps}

brief.head: The plotting poet-king
brief.text: Bahadur Shah Zafar, usu­ally shown as a weak poet-king, was in fact “a schemer and a plot­ter” who “con­tained mul­ti­tudes”, Amit Varma said, draw­ing on Swapna Liddle. {#zafar}

brief.head: In praise of lust
brief.text: Amit Varma prefers lust to love, be­cause lust is hon­est. Love, he said, can be a cover for want­ing sta­tus, so­cial ac­cep­tance or com­pan­ion­ship with a par­tic­u­lar kind of per­son. {043-C12}

brief.head: Safe in harbour
brief.text: A ship is safe in the har­bour, Ajay Shah said, but that is not what ships are for. Germany’s new fleet sat out the First World War in dock. {043-J15}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah pitch six more films
lead.head: Lights, camera, plutonium

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 43

body: Ajay Shah opened by thank­ing lis­ten­ers for “wast­ing your life lis­ten­ing to us ram­bling”. Amit Varma ob­jected at once. “They’re not wast­ing their lives,” he said. “We are going to tell them sto­ries.”
It was the hosts’ fourth episode of sto­ries that should be films. Varma brought two fic­tions and a slice of true his­tory; Shah brought three true tales, the last of them only a scene.
## Into the open sea

Varma’s first pitch grew from a thought ex­per­i­ment by the en­tre­pre­neur Deepak VS: re­place the IIT en­trance exam with a swim­ming test. By the sec­ond year, Deepak warned, Kota would be run­ning swim­ming classes. {043-C01}
In Varma’s film, a boy who loves en­gi­neer­ing is trapped on a tread­mill of IIT-sized pools. He finds joy only in the open sea, fails his exam, and swims out past the dan­ger marker into a storm.
Shah called it “a great metaphor for our times”, but asked for a more re­demp­tive story. “Redemption, you want a happy story,” Varma replied. “We all die.” {043-J01}
## Real, not rea­son­able
Shah’s of­fer­ing was a Cold War tale. In the 1950s, he said, the CIA wanted to watch China’s nu­clear tests from a Himalayan sum­mit, with a plu­to­nium bat­tery to power the lis­ten­ing post.
The equip­ment was lashed to rocks on Nanda Devi as a storm came in. When the climbers re­turned, it was gone. It has never been found.
“This is your re­demp­tive story,” Varma said.
Shah replied: “The dif­fer­ence be­tween re­al­ity and fic­tion is that re­al­ity is not obliged to be rea­son­able.” {043-C02}
Varma replied with true his­tory of his own: Delhi be­tween 1803 and 1857, drawn from Swapna Liddle’s *The Broken Script*.

In those fifty years Persian van­ished as the lan­guage of power, print­ing presses ar­rived, and po­etry sold news­pa­pers. At Delhi College, Western knowl­edge was taught in Hindustani. “It’s like we’re teach­ing the Magna Carta,” Shah said, “but we’re doing it in Urdu.”
## Ships, sheep and vlogs
Shah then told of the German fleet that sat out the First World War in dock and was meant to be de­liv­ered to Britain at Scapa Flow. Its sailors blew it up in­stead.
That raised a ques­tion Varma left open: should a sol­dier obey or­ders, when we would cheer the same de­fi­ance had the sides been re­versed? {043-C07}
The wrecks, Shah added, now sup­ply the pre-nuclear steel for Geiger coun­ters, in­clud­ing those that searched Nanda Devi. “The ta­pes­try of the world brings ev­ery­thing to­gether,” he said.

Varma’s last pitch was a low-budget film told only through vlogs, about an ev­ery­day vlog­ger who falls for an an­drog­y­nous new­comer who seems wholly con­structed, and may be the only one being true to them­selves.
That set off a de­bate about au­then­tic­ity. Shah called it “the lazi­est pose”. Varma said char­ac­ter is not a rock but a river. {043-C10}
Shah closed with Mussolini’s sol­diers in Ethiopia in 1935, who re­belled over bad food and were sent live sheep by para­chute. “The sheep is a life sup­port sys­tem,” he ex­plained.
Varma called it “the great­est scene of all time”, then signed off with a plea to read good books, fic­tion or not: “Everything, my friends, is sto­ries.”

second.label: A Soviet side story
second.head: Hot property, cold guard
second.deck: Ajay Shah on a Soviet guard who learned that plutonium is always warm

pic.caption: Lavrentiy Beria, head of the Soviet NKVD, circa 1938–1940

body: During the Soviet atom bomb project, Ajay Shah said, the physi­cists were watched by NKVD jail­ers under Beria, who did not trust them. If the first test failed, the guards had or­ders to shoot every physi­cist.

One day a guard burst in on a physi­cist hold­ing a piece of metal and ac­cused him of pass­ing off stain­less steel as plu­to­nium. “You got to be a com­mu­nist to know the phrase ma­lin­gerer,” Shah re­marked. {043-J05}

The physi­cist re­mem­bered that plu­to­nium is al­ways warm from decay, and sent the guard out into minus twenty de­grees hold­ing it. Half an hour later the guard’s ear­lobes had frost­bite. The metal was still warm, and the physi­cist won a day’s re­prieve. {043-S03}

quote.text: Okay, fine, then I’ll kill you to­mor­row.

third.head: All the news fit to rhyme

pic.caption: Amit Varma on poetry that sold newspapers

body: What did every Delhi news­pa­per need in order to sell, Amit Varma asked. Ajay Shah guessed gos­sip and celebrity scan­dal. The an­swer, in Delhi then, was po­etry. {043-S07}

“Poets, in a sense, were the great pub­lic fig­ures of their time,” Varma said. One typ­i­cal issue of the *Delhi Urdu Akhbar* car­ried news from as far afield as Afghanistan, France and Russia. In 1841 it ran an ed­i­to­rial ar­gu­ing for widow re­mar­riage. {#widow}

Mushairas were ev­ery­where, and the verses re­cited at them were printed as tazki­ras. These sold so well that one Karimuddin, who did not care for po­etry, began hold­ing reg­u­lar mushairas just so he could pub­lish them.
Another tazkira opened with an essay teach­ing read­ers what metre is and how to use a metaphor. Early English news­pa­pers, Varma noted, were gos­sip and tabloid ma­te­rial.

p2.title: Morals of the story
p2.deck: Each pitch hid an argument: about tests, truth, language, duty and the self

quote.text: To hell with the swim­ming pool. Why should I stay in my lane?

box.title: The book behind the series
box.text: Amit Varma’s Delhi pitch rests on Swapna Liddle’s *The Broken Script*, which he called one of the finest his­tory books he has read in re­cent years, and the best book of quasi-Mughal his­tory he has come across. {043-R01}

sections.label: The first film
sections.head: The lane less travelled
sections.caption: the boy who left his lane
body: Amit Varma’s first story began with a thought ex­per­i­ment from Deepak VS, a Bangalore en­tre­pre­neur in his mid-twenties. Replace the IIT en­trance test with a swim­ming test, Deepak said, and the en­gi­neers would be just as good.

Varma got car­ried away and said they would be bet­ter, since what the exam re­ally se­lects for is “hunger, pas­sion, ini­tia­tive”. Deepak, “like a wise man, even though he is a young man”, cor­rected him. By the sec­ond year the sys­tem would be gamed again, with Kota run­ning swim­ming classes and bill­boards of coaches in Speedos. {043-C01}
## Out past the marker

Varma’s film is set a year or two into the new regime. Its hero has an engineer’s mind but must slog through IIT-sized pools against boys who care noth­ing for en­gi­neer­ing. The per­son he is fall­ing for reaches across from the next lane and hits him to get ahead.

He es­capes to the sea and, for the first time, en­joys swim­ming. His coach­ing grades slide, he fails, and his mother stops talk­ing to him. He swims out past the dan­ger marker into a gath­er­ing storm. {043-S01}
Ajay Shah found it “deep and al­le­gor­i­cal”, un­like “silly TV se­ri­als about chil­dren pre­par­ing in Kota”. {043-J20}
~ Varma closed the chap­ter with one of his favourite poems, Stevie Smith’s *Not Waving but Drowning*, which ends: “I was much too far out all my life, and not wav­ing but drown­ing.” {043-R04}

quote.text: To hell with the swim­ming pool. Why should I stay in my lane?

sections.label: The second film
sections.head: Word soup, every word true
sections.caption: a story that is all true
body: Ajay Shah promised a story with a trou­bling end in which “every word of it is true”: a CIA plu­to­nium bat­tery lost on Nanda Devi. Then he drew the moral. “The dif­fer­ence be­tween re­al­ity and fic­tion is that re­al­ity is not obliged to be rea­son­able.” {043-C02}

To prove it, he played a pitch meet­ing with Amit Varma as the movie mogul grant­ing him two min­utes. America, India, CIA, China, plu­to­nium, tens of mil­lions at risk in UP, hip­pies at Nanda Devi: Varma, he said, would call it word soup. {043-J03}
## Still up there

The dan­ger has not passed. One the­ory, Shah said, is that the bat­tery, al­ways warm from ra­dioac­tive decay, melted its way hun­dreds of me­tres into the glacier and lodged in rock. “The damn thing has a half life of thou­sands of years,” he said. {#halflife}

Varma was taken with the image of plu­to­nium “sink­ing, sink­ing, sink­ing” through an ice-covered moun­tain, and with the human drama of the climbers and the gov­ern­ment. He also pro­posed mer­chan­dise for the co-producers: a T-shirt read­ing “Okay, fine, I’ll kill you to­mor­row”, the line of a Soviet guard in Shah’s side story. {043-J02}
~ Shah ad­vised lis­ten­ers to warn their great-great-grandchildren off the Gangetic plain. Varma pointed out that gen­tle read­ers do not have great-great-grandchildren.

quote.text: Gentle reader, you should tell your great great grand­chil­dren don’t live in the Gangetic plain.

sections.label: The web series
sections.head: A city loses its language
sections.caption: Delhi in churn, 1803 to 1857
body: Amit Varma’s third pitch was a web se­ries set in Delhi be­tween 1803, when the East India Company won the sec­ond Anglo-Maratha war, and 1857. {#maratha} The Mughals ruled in name; the Company held the power.

What gripped him most was some­thing that rarely hap­pens in human his­tory: the lin­gua franca changed. Persian held the place English holds in India today, “nobody’s mother tongue” but the lan­guage of power. Within fifty years it was out.
“If you are a kid who’s ten years old,” he said, “you look at your par­ents and they’re com­pletely help­less in the new world.” {043-C03}
## Western knowl­edge, local tongue
Printing presses spread at the same time. “When you write down a word, you os­sify it,” Varma said: print brings sta­bil­ity but loses some of the flux of a spon­ta­neous order. {043-C04}

Delhi College’s en­dow­ment came from one Fazal Ali, on con­di­tion that teach­ing be in local lan­guages. So Western knowl­edge was taught in Hindustani, which had no tech­ni­cal terms for it, “a lot of which is a prob­lem to this day”. {043-C05}

~ The cast was full of con­tra­dic­tions. Ghalib, al­ready a leg­end, ran from a money­len­der and tried to suck up to the British. Raja Ram Mohan Roy, a fear­less re­former, pleaded with a Mughal em­peror in ob­se­quious terms. {043-C06}

quote.text: It seems to me to be a great locus of all this, be­cause you have the col­li­sion of the worlds there.

sections.label: The fourth film
sections.head: Return to sender
sections.caption: the navy that was never delivered
body: Ajay Shah asked lis­ten­ers to imag­ine an Amazon de­liv­ery, then “a de­liv­ery of a navy”. {043-J07} Under the Treaty of Versailles, Germany’s freshly minted fleet was to be handed to Britain at Scapa Flow. Its sailors sank it in­stead.

Amit Varma raised the hard ques­tion. A sol­dier, he said, should fol­low or­ders, be­cause “if ev­ery­one starts ra­tio­nal­iz­ing like that, you kinda get screwed”. Yet had England lost and the Nazis been tak­ing its navy, we would cheer the sol­dier who blew it up. {043-C07}
That, Shah said, made it “lovely movie ma­te­rial”: some sailors must have ar­gued that a deal is a deal, oth­ers that a navy that had never fought should not be given away.
## A mir­ror in Algeria
He set it be­side Mers-el-Kébir in Algeria, from an ear­lier episode. There French sailors chose to obey or­ders rather than join the British, who opened fire. Thousands died.

Then he tied the threads. Since nu­clear test­ing began, nearly all new steel has been con­tam­i­nated, so Geiger coun­ters need steel made be­fore the bomb, cut by divers from the wrecks at Scapa Flow. The coun­ters that searched Nanda Devi were made of it. {043-S09}
~ Varma called it mar­vel­lous. The uni­verse, Shah al­lowed, would have found some other source, “but it is just so sweet that these sto­ries tie to­gether”.

quote.text: Why the hell will we give a freshly minted navy that has never fought a war?

sections.label: The fifth film
sections.head: When the mask becomes the face
sections.caption: authenticity and love
body: Amit Varma’s fifth pitch was a low-budget film made en­tirely of vlogs, with no third-person cam­era. Its show­piece is a vloggers’ Mexican stand­off, cam­eras in place of guns, pulling back into a hall of mir­rors. {043-J14}

But, he said, “the crux of the story al­ways has to do with love”. An ev­ery­day, lik­able vlog­ger falls for a new­comer who seems wholly con­structed: beau­ti­ful, an­drog­y­nous, im­pos­si­ble to pin down.

Love, in Iris Murdoch’s words as Varma quoted them, is “the ex­tremely dif­fi­cult re­al­iza­tion that some­one other than one­self is real”. We all live with main char­ac­ter syn­drome, he said, until love makes some­one else real. {043-C11}
Varma wants the viewer to see, in the end, that the an­drog­y­nous vlog­ger is the one being true to them­selves. How the film gets there, he ad­mit­ted, he has not thought of yet. {043-J10}
## Without ef­fort
Ajay Shah pressed him on au­then­tic­ity. “There is only one per­son that I can be with­out ef­fort, and that is me,” Shah said, and he de­fined au­then­tic­ity as the lazi­est pose. {043-C09}
~ Varma ques­tioned the word it­self. Skip break­fast and the chem­istry of the brain shifts by evening. And a pose you keep work­ing at be­comes yours: “the mask be­comes a face often”.

quote.text: We think my char­ac­ter is a rock. No, it isn’t. My char­ac­ter is a river.

But you re­al­ize that there are dif­fer­ent cur­rents that we swim in at the same time. Some are the cur­rents of his­tory, some are the cur­rents of so­ci­ety, and there’s all this other per­sonal stuff hap­pen­ing.

p3.title: Stranger than fiction
p3.deck: Lost plutonium, a sunken fleet, falling sheep and a forgotten mathematician

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s Cold War tale from the Himalayas
stories.head: Last seen on Nanda Devi
body: In the 1950s China was on its way to a nu­clear weapon, and its tests would nat­u­rally take place on the Tibetan plateau. Spy satel­lites could not yet watch it, Ajay Shah said. So the CIA came to India with a propo­si­tion.

An Indian Army team had just climbed Kanchenjunga. The Americans wanted to haul equip­ment to its sum­mit, “some twenty eight thou­sand feet high”, and spend years gath­er­ing dust from the air and mea­sur­ing ra­dioac­tiv­ity over Tibet. {#summit} Power would come from a bat­tery driven by plu­to­nium decay.
The Indian climbers, back from the sum­mit a month ear­lier, flatly re­fused. Nobody, they said, could carry a 70-kilogram bat­tery up Kanchenjunga. {#battery} They pro­posed Nanda Devi in­stead.

Elite American climbers were ap­proached by the CIA one by one: all ex­penses paid, total se­crecy. On the sec­ond at­tempt, with a storm com­ing, the team lashed the equip­ment to rocks at a spot they mem­o­rised, since there was no GPS, and ran down. When they re­turned, the place was un­recog­nis­able and the equip­ment was gone.
It was never found. If its plu­to­nium ever reached the Ganga, Shah said, tens of mil­lions of peo­ple in the Gangetic plain would die. {043-S02}
India needed a cover story. Too many hik­ers and hip­pies, it said, were dam­ag­ing a pre­cious bio­di­ver­sity re­serve. Nanda Devi was shut to all, and for years searched with Geiger coun­ters.
~ One the­ory is that the Chinese climbed up from their side and took it. Another is that the warm plu­to­nium melted its way hun­dreds of me­tres into the glacier, where it sits still.
stories.why: A Cold War spy plan and an en­vi­ron­men­tal clo­sure turned out to be one story. Reality, Shah said, is not obliged to be rea­son­able, and this one has not ended: the plu­to­nium will keep going for thou­sands of years. {043-C02}
stories.postscript: Nanda Devi, Shah added, is one of the world’s most glo­ri­ous hik­ing re­gions. Readers who have never hiked must “run, not walk”.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the plutonium lost on Nanda Devi

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a fleet that would not be delivered
stories.head: Sunk costs at Scapa Flow
body: Germany built a navy to chal­lenge the Royal Navy, Ajay Shah said, but in 1914 it was not ready. Its shiny new ships, prob­a­bly half the size of the British fleet, sat out the First World War in dock. {#halfsize}

The Treaty of Versailles capped the German army at 100,000 men, with no tanks and no navy. {#versailles} More than a hun­dred ships and more than a hun­dred sub­marines were to be de­liv­ered to Britain at Scapa Flow, at the top of Scotland.

The German sailors had other plans. They mounted ex­plo­sives in their ships, and one by one some­thing like sev­enty or eighty big war­ships blew up and sank. {043-S08} Many died, be­cause the evac­u­a­tions had not been planned.
~ In the days be­fore the han­dover, Shah noted, the sailors had been treated pet­tily, with­out enough food or san­i­ta­tion.

quote.text: You may have signed the treaty of Versailles. We refuse. We’re not giv­ing you the ships.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the scuttling at Scapa Flow

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s scene for the writers of the world
stories.head: Dinner arrives by parachute
body: In 1935, Ajay Shah said, Mussolini had delu­sions of grandeur. {#mussolini} He meant to recre­ate the Roman Empire, and led an in­va­sion of what is now Ethiopia and Somalia.

His sol­diers were “just guys who wanted to have a good time”. Their hearts were not in the fight, nor were their stom­achs, and out in the boon­docks groups of them re­belled over bad mil­i­tary food. {043-J11}

The fix: sheep from Italy were loaded onto planes, strapped to para­chutes and dropped one by one over the army camps, and a near mutiny was staved off. Why not drop boxes of meat, Amit Varma asked. “The sheep is a life sup­port sys­tem,” Shah said. “It has an im­mune sys­tem. It keeps the meat fresh.” {043-S11}
~ At least one pho­to­graph sur­vives, Shah said: “a very blurry, bad black and white photo”. {#photo}
stories.why: A near mutiny was averted by solv­ing a food prob­lem, with a fix as ab­surd as it was work­able. Shah of­fered it as a scene, not a full story, for the world’s writ­ers to build on.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the parachuting sheep

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a genius history mislaid
stories.head: The Ramanujan who missed his Hardy
body: Ramchandra, born in 1821, taught at Delhi College and tried to ex­plain the rules of cal­cu­lus using al­ge­bra. {043-S05}

His trea­tise reached the British math­e­ma­ti­cian Augustus De Morgan, who was blown away and tried his best to pro­mote him. Amit Varma re­called a ref­er­ence call­ing the pair the Hardy and Ramanujan of their age, ex­cept that Hardy suc­ceeded and De Morgan could not.

Ramchandra was also a fear­less ra­tio­nal­ist. He spoke out against tra­di­tional medicine and against every re­li­gion, local and Western, and started jour­nal after jour­nal to get his ideas to the peo­ple. Then, hav­ing just crossed thirty in 1852, he con­verted to Christianity, which noth­ing he had writ­ten ex­plains. {#convert}
~ After 1857, Varma said, he be­came “a head­mas­ter of some ran­dom school”.
stories.why: Genius alone did not de­cide who be­came fa­mous: pa­tron­age and the up­heaval of 1857 mat­tered too. And even a well-documented life, Varma found, can stay a mys­tery, as Ramchandra’s con­ver­sion shows.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Ramchandra, the forgotten mathematician

quiz.q: In Deepak VS’s thought experiment, what would replace the IIT entrance exam?
quiz.a: A swim­ming test, though by the sec­ond year Kota would be run­ning swim­ming classes.

quiz.q: Why did the CIA’s listening post move from Kanchenjunga to Nanda Devi?
quiz.a: Indian climbers said no­body could carry a 70 kg bat­tery up Kanchenjunga.

quiz.q: How did a Soviet physicist prove to a suspicious guard that his metal was plutonium?
quiz.a: The guard held it out­side at minus twenty for half an hour; it stayed warm.

quiz.q: What condition did Fazal Ali attach to his endowment of Delhi College?
quiz.a: That teach­ing be in local lan­guages, so Western knowl­edge was taught in Hindustani.

quiz.q: Why do sensitive Geiger counters need steel from the wrecks at Scapa Flow?
quiz.a: Newer steel car­ries ra­dioac­tive dust from bomb tests; the sunken fleet’s steel pre­dates them.

quiz.q: Why did Mussolini’s army drop live sheep rather than boxes of meat on its camps?
quiz.a: Refrigeration was lim­ited, and a live sheep, a ‘life sup­port system’, kept the meat fresh.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 43. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Benito Mussolini (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Lavrentiy Beria (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Mirza Ghalib (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Ram Mohan Roy (Rembrandt Peale, public domain); Stevie Smith (Akshay Nagaraju B, CC BY-SA 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Deepak VS, an en­tre­pre­neur in his mid-twenties whom Amit calls an in­cred­i­bly fine thinker, is al­ways throw­ing out thought ex­per­i­ments that de­nor­malise things; he pointed out that any new en­trance test would be gamed within a year.

shelf.title: Inside the CIA Mission to Haul Plutonium Up the Himalayas
shelf.creator: Robert Beckhusen

shelf.title: Are You Just One Version of Yourself? (Episode 3, Everything is Everything)

shelf.why: On whether char­ac­ter is con­tin­gent and whether we can ever know our­selves: a small change in brain chem­istry, as with Phineas Gage, can make you a dif­fer­ent per­son.

shelf.title: The Reformers (Episode 28, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: More true sto­ries pitched as films, in the for­mat of the Stories That Should Be Films se­ries.

laughs.text: Ajay asks for a re­demp­tive end­ing after the drown­ing story, and Amit replies: ‘Redemption, you want a happy story. We all die.’ Then Ajay de­liv­ers a tale of lost plu­to­nium that could poi­son the Gangetic plain, and Amit re­torts: ‘This is your re­demp­tive story.’

Amit pro­poses mer­chan­dise for their joint pro­duc­tion: a T-shirt read­ing ‘Okay, fine, I’ll kill you to­mor­row,’ the Soviet guard’s ver­dict after the plu­to­nium proved it­self. He calls it ‘the best T-shirt line ever.’
Ajay: ‘Gentle reader, you should tell your great great grand­chil­dren don’t live in the Gangetic plain.’ Amit: ‘Gentle reader don’t have great great grand­chil­dren.’
Amit in­sists he won’t give spoil­ers about how the vlog­ging film ends, then ad­mits: ‘But ac­tu­ally the truth is I haven’t thought of that yet.’

Ajay voices the Italian sol­diers in Ethiopia: ‘Mamma Mia... I’ll go out to far away coun­tries and I’ll kill strangers, but you gotta feed me.’ When Amit asks why not drop boxes of meat, Ajay ex­plains the sheep is ‘a life sup­port sys­tem,’ and Amit adds that ‘it can keep the sol­diers com­pany in other ways.’
Stevie Smith’s ‘Not Waving but Drowning’ (‘I was much too far out all my life, and not wav­ing but drowning’), read as the coda to the IIT-swimmer story.
Iris Murdoch: ‘Love is the ex­tremely dif­fi­cult re­al­iza­tion that some­one other than one­self is real,’ used to frame the vlog­ger who falls in love.
